Baby & Child

Brain tumor types in children: understanding the names

Updated: November 10, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Hearing that a child has a brain tumor can leave a family facing unfamiliar words before they have had time to understand what is happening. “Brain tumor” describes a broad group of conditions. The exact type, where it is growing and its biological features are more useful than the name alone when discussing what comes next.

Location is part of the explanation

The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system, or CNS. The cerebrum supports thinking, language and voluntary movement; the cerebellum helps coordinate movement and balance. The brainstem links the brain to the spinal cord and supports vital functions such as breathing and swallowing. A tumor’s position helps explain which functions may be affected, but symptoms cannot identify its type. Spinal tumors may affect movement, sensation or bowel and bladder function.

Some tumors develop near the pathways for vision or the structures that control hormones. Others affect the fluid-filled spaces called ventricles. Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, can cause hydrocephalus: an abnormal fluid buildup that can raise pressure. A small tumor in a sensitive location may therefore cause serious problems even when it grows slowly. Size alone does not tell the whole story.

Type, grade and spread answer different questions

The type names the disease. A CNS WHO grade, when assigned, describes biological behavior using the tumor’s appearance and sometimes molecular findings. A higher grade generally signals more aggressive behavior within that tumor type. Grade is not the same as stage or the extent of spread. Different tumor types with the same grade can have very different treatment responses and outcomes.

“Benign” means noncancerous; it does not mean harmless inside the skull. A noncancerous tumor can press on important tissue, disrupt hormone production or obstruct fluid flow. Conversely, “malignant” does not mean that nothing can be done. Ask the team to explain the exact diagnosis, whether it has spread and which features matter for this child, rather than using a single grade to predict their future.

Astrocytomas and other gliomas form a varied family

Gliomas are associated with the supporting cells of the nervous system. Astrocytoma is a familiar name within this family, but it does not describe one uniform illness. Childhood gliomas can occur in many parts of the brain or spinal cord and include slow-growing and aggressive diseases. They are not all centered in the pons, a part of the brainstem, and they do not all spread in the same way.

Modern reports distinguish pediatric-type diffuse low-grade and high-grade gliomas from circumscribed astrocytic tumors. “Diffuse” describes growth among surrounding tissue; “circumscribed” describes a more defined growth pattern. These are useful distinctions, not a promise about whether surgery is possible. A report may include a molecular name, such as diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered. That specific diagnosis should not be applied to every tumor in the brainstem.

Pilocytic astrocytoma and PXA are not interchangeable

Pilocytic astrocytoma is a CNS WHO grade 1 tumor and is often relatively slow growing. It commonly occurs in the cerebellum, but can also involve the visual pathways, hypothalamus or brainstem. Its outlook and the safest approach depend partly on its location. A tumor close to structures controlling vision or other essential functions may be difficult to remove completely without causing harm.

Pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma, shortened to PXA, is a different astrocytic tumor, often near the surface of the cerebral hemispheres. It can be grade 2 or grade 3. Certain BRAF changes are common, but cannot be assumed from the name alone. PXA should not simply be grouped with tumors containing both neuronal and glial elements. If similar names appear on two reports, ask whether the diagnosis was refined after further tissue testing.

Embryonal tumors and the older term PNET

PNET, or primitive neuroectodermal tumor, is an older umbrella term. Tumors once collected under that label are now separated using more specific tissue and molecular findings. An old report or webpage saying “PNET” may therefore not identify the diagnosis used by a specialist today. Ask for the current integrated diagnosis before comparing treatment stories or survival figures.

Medulloblastoma is an embryonal tumor that usually starts in the cerebellum and can spread through CSF. Its molecular groups include WNT-activated, SHH-activated and the non-WNT/non-SHH groups commonly called groups 3 and 4. Pineoblastoma is a separate aggressive tumor of the pineal region deep in the brain. It is not another name for medulloblastoma, and not every pineal-region tumor is a pineoblastoma. These distinctions can substantially change the discussion of care.

Ependymoma: site and molecular group matter

Ependymomas are related to cells lining the brain’s ventricles and the spinal cord’s central canal. They can arise in the upper brain (supratentorial), the lower back part of the brain (posterior fossa), or the spine. An ependymoma can obstruct CSF circulation or spread within the CNS; it is misleading to say these tumors never affect nearby brain tissue or never spread.

Classification combines location, tissue appearance and molecular features. Older wording such as “anaplastic ependymoma” may still appear in records, but is no longer a separate named type in the 2021 WHO classification. Myxopapillary ependymoma, often found low in the spinal canal, is now classified as grade 2 rather than grade 1. Fluid drainage may be needed when a tumor causes hydrocephalus, but a shunt is not automatically required for every child.

Craniopharyngioma can affect vision and hormones

Craniopharyngioma usually develops near the pituitary gland and hypothalamus, close to the nerves involved in vision. It often contains both solid tissue and fluid-filled cysts. Although noncancerous, it can affect sight, growth, puberty, thirst, weight and hormone production. These effects explain why a child may need eye and hormone specialists as well as a brain-tumor team.

The cause is often unknown, and there are no established risk factors for childhood craniopharyngioma. It should not routinely be described to families as an inherited disease. Changes found in tumor cells do not automatically mean that a parent passed on the condition. Treatment and follow-up must account for the tumor’s position and the risk of damaging nearby structures; problems with hormones or vision may continue even after tumor treatment.

Oligodendroglioma needs a specific molecular definition

Oligodendroglioma is much more often diagnosed in adults and is uncommon in children. Under modern classification, the diagnosis requires an IDH gene mutation together with loss of particular parts of chromosomes 1 and 19, called 1p/19q codeletion. Cells looking like oligodendrocytes under a microscope are not enough on their own to establish this diagnosis.

Oligodendrogliomas can be grade 2 or grade 3. A grade 2 tumor may grow slowly but still extend into surrounding tissue; grade 3 disease behaves more aggressively. A childhood tumor with a similar microscopic appearance may belong to a different molecular group. Families should therefore use the complete pathology wording when seeking information, and avoid applying adult outcome statistics to a child.

Schwannoma arises from nerve-covering cells

Schwannomas develop from cells that support and insulate nerves. A vestibular schwannoma affects the nerve involved in hearing and balance; it is also called an acoustic neuroma. It is usually noncancerous and slow growing, but its position can cause hearing loss, imbalance or pressure on nearby structures. Hearing changes alone do not diagnose it, because many more common ear conditions can cause similar symptoms.

Some schwannomas occur as part of a tumor-predisposition condition. The name NF2-related schwannomatosis now replaces neurofibromatosis type 2 in current terminology. Multiple tumors, tumors on both hearing-and-balance nerves or other relevant findings may prompt specialist genetic assessment. This is different from assuming every schwannoma is inherited. The genetics team can explain which tests are useful and whether any relatives need evaluation.

Choroid plexus tumors are not all benign

The choroid plexus is tissue within the ventricles that produces CSF. Its tumors include choroid plexus papilloma, atypical choroid plexus papilloma and choroid plexus carcinoma. These names correspond to grades 1, 2 and 3 respectively. Papillomas are noncancerous; atypical papillomas have a greater tendency to recur. Carcinomas are malignant and more likely to spread within the CNS.

A choroid plexus tumor can cause hydrocephalus through excess fluid production or interference with normal flow. This helps explain why fluid-pressure treatment may be urgent even before a family understands the full tumor name. The care plan depends on the exact type, the child’s age, location and other findings. “A tumor in the ventricle” is a location description, not enough information to identify its behavior.

Mixed and glioneuronal labels need clarification

Ganglioglioma and dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumor, often abbreviated DNET, are examples of glioneuronal tumors, which have neuronal and glial components. They are distinct from a vague description such as “mixed glioma.” Modern classification uses tissue and molecular findings to identify diseases that older microscopic descriptions sometimes grouped together. A more precise name can help the team explain what is known and what remains uncertain.

Ask for a copy of the final pathology report and an explanation of any pending molecular tests. The integrated diagnosis brings together the relevant findings; it may be more specific than an early scan impression or preliminary tissue report. If tissue cannot safely be obtained, some diagnoses rely on clinical findings and imaging instead. Whether a biopsy is needed is a specialist decision, not a rule that every child must undergo the same procedure.

Symptoms still need assessment, whatever the name

A tumor list cannot determine the cause of a child’s symptoms. Arrange medical assessment for persistent or worsening neurological changes. Seek urgent help for a child’s headache with vomiting or vision problems, a headache that is worsening or waking them at night, or one triggered by coughing or bending. These symptoms have causes other than tumors, but should not be dismissed while searching for a matching tumor type.

Call emergency services for a first seizure in progress, a seizure lasting more than five minutes or longer than usual, or repeated seizures without recovery. Emergency assessment is also needed for a headache with new weakness, difficulty speaking or walking, confusion, unusual drowsiness, sudden extremely severe pain or loss of vision. If a suspected first seizure has stopped and the child has not been assessed, obtain urgent medical advice. Follow any existing seizure emergency plan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the team to write down the integrated diagnosis, location, grade if assigned, and any pending molecular results.

Discuss what the findings mean for this child’s function and treatment; avoid comparing unrelated tumors or adult survival figures.

Keep a clear contact and emergency plan for new symptoms, including any individualized seizure instructions.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize questions and explanations from the care team. It cannot identify a tumor from symptoms or images, interpret a pathology report independently or predict a child’s outcome.

When to seek help

Seek urgent advice for worsening childhood headache, headache with vomiting or vision problems, or a suspected first seizure that has stopped without assessment. A first seizure in progress, prolonged or repeated seizures without recovery, or headache with new weakness, speech or walking difficulty, confusion, unusual drowsiness or loss of vision requires emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: November 10, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The exact tumor type, location and molecular findings matter alongside grade.
  • A noncancerous brain tumor can still threaten vision, hormones, movement or fluid circulation.
  • Astrocytoma, ependymoma, medulloblastoma and other tumor names describe different diseases.
  • Older terms such as PNET may need clarification against the current pathology report.
  • Use the child’s specialist team for individual prognosis and seek timely care for new neurological symptoms.

Frequently asked questions

What are the main types of brain tumors in children?

They include several kinds of glioma, such as astrocytoma, as well as medulloblastoma, ependymoma, craniopharyngioma and other rarer tumors. This is not a complete diagnostic list. Some names describe a family of diseases, so the final tissue and molecular diagnosis is more useful than a broad label.

Do all astrocytomas behave the same way?

No. Astrocytic tumors range from relatively slow-growing diseases such as pilocytic astrocytoma to aggressive tumors. Their location and molecular findings also matter. Astrocytomas are not all confined to the brainstem, and one child’s experience cannot reliably predict another’s.

Can a benign brain tumor be serious?

Yes. A noncancerous tumor can press on important structures or block cerebrospinal fluid flow. It may need treatment and long-term follow-up even though it does not behave like an aggressive cancer. “Benign” does not mean that symptoms can be ignored.

What is craniopharyngioma?

It is a usually cystic and solid, noncancerous tumor near the pituitary gland and hypothalamus. It can affect sight, growth and hormone control. Childhood cases have no established risk factors and should not routinely be presented as inherited. Specialist follow-up may be needed for continuing hormonal or visual problems.

Is a grade 4 tumor the same as stage 4 cancer?

No. Grade concerns the tumor’s biological features; stage or spread concerns where disease is present. Brain tumors do not all use the same staging system. A grade alone cannot give an individual prognosis or tell you that the tumor has spread throughout the body.

Why has the tumor name changed after more tests?

Microscopic examination and molecular tests may refine an initial diagnosis. Classification has also changed over time, including the older PNET umbrella label. Ask whether the change reflects new laboratory information, updated terminology or a genuine change in the disease.

Does a gene change in the tumor mean other children in the family are at risk?

Not automatically. A change confined to tumor cells is different from an inherited predisposition. Some tumor patterns do warrant genetic assessment, including certain schwannoma presentations. The team should explain whether family testing is relevant rather than assuming it is needed for every tumor.

Can symptoms or an online scan image identify the tumor type?

No. Symptoms overlap between tumor types and many conditions that are not tumors. Scans help locate a problem, while tissue and molecular analysis often refine the diagnosis when sampling is appropriate. New neurological symptoms need clinical assessment; emergency warning signs should not wait for online interpretation.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
